author: jsonbored
body:
Closes metagraphed-infra#382 — part 1 of metagraphed-infra#353, for the one lane that meets its bar.

#353 set the condition: **≥5 consecutive clean queued passes**, then the inline branch goes and the route is enqueue-only.

`account-balances` was re-cut onto `sync-batches` at 2026-08-06 08:45Z (#9641). **Six consecutive complete passes since**, read from `account_balances_passes` on production D1:

```
08-07 04:38:16Z  364,817 / 364,817   completed
08-07 00:28:39Z  372,569 / 364,819   completed   ← at-least-once overshoot, expected
08-06 18:28:39Z  364,747 / 364,747   completed
08-06 12:28:40Z  364,668 / 364,668   completed
08-06 11:14:02Z  364,654 / 364,654   completed
08-06 10:38:44Z  364,644 / 364,644   completed
```

This is **the lane that caused the original incident** — `D1_ERROR: D1 DB is overloaded` aborted a pass at 147,000 of 364,000 rows and took `wallet-auth` and `tao-usd-index` down with it on the shared database. That is why its rollback was worth keeping longest, and why the evidence is quoted rather than summarised.

## What comes out

Four things #353 listed, plus one it did not:

| removed | |
|---|---|
| the `syncLaneUsesQueue` guard | |
| the `!env.METAGRAPH_HEALTH_DB` 503 | the route no longer touches D1 at all |
| `writeAccountBalancesToD1` + its try/catch | the write is the consumer's |
| `stores: ["d1"]`, `d1_statements` | no statement count to report |
| **`mirrorLedgerToNeon`** | **not anticipated by the issue** — the lane has two writers and both mirrored; the consumer's is now the only one |

## Rollback is no longer a flag, and the route says so

Dropping the lane from `SYNC_QUEUE_LANES` does **not** restore a D1 path any more — it enqueues to a queue nothing is routed to. So an absent `SYNC_BATCHES` binding is a **loud 503** rather than a route that accepts rows it cannot deliver, and **reverting this commit is the rollback**.

The `400`-before-`503` ordering is preserved deliberately: a malformed body is the caller's fault whether or not a binding happens to be present.

## The tests are the substantive part

The route's suite asserts real write behaviour *through the route*: latest-capture-wins, an account absent from a later batch is kept, a whole batch is one statement, and the entire `pass_total` completeness set. Deleting the inline write would have left those either failing or — worse — quietly rewritten into assertions about a code path production no longer takes.

Instead, `postAndConsume` posts and then drives what was enqueued through the **real `worker.queue` consumer**. Same assertions, same guarantees, now against the path that actually runs. 32 call sites moved; the queue-routing suite keeps raw `post`, because those tests are about the route's own behaviour.

Six route-response tests changed shape for real reasons, each stated inline:

- `stores: ["queue"]` and no `d1_statements`
- the required-binding test now targets `SYNC_BATCHES`, not `METAGRAPH_HEALTH_DB`
- "a D1 failure is a 502" became "a failed **enqueue** is a 502" — a D1 write failure is no longer the route's failure mode at all; the consumer **retries** rather than answering the producer, which is the point of the transport moving (covered end to end in `data-api-sync-queue-consumer.test.ts`)
- "an un-opted deployment still writes D1" became "an unbound queue is a loud 503, not a silent drop" — there is no un-opted deployment for this lane any more

## Validation

```
npm run typecheck    # clean
npm run lint         # clean
npx prettier --check # clean
npx vitest run tests/data-api-account-balances-d1.test.ts \
  tests/data-api-sync-queue-consumer.test.ts tests/sync-batch-queue.test.ts tests/top-holders.test.ts
# 135 passed
```

Patch coverage by intersecting the diff with a v8 report over `workers/data-api.ts`: **0 uncovered statements, 0 uncovered branches** (33 changed lines).

## Not in scope

The other three routed lanes are untouched. `hotkey-alpha` has one queued pass (24h timer — that is every tick it has had), and `validator-nominator-counts` / `nominator-positions` have **no pass table at all**, so #353's bar cannot be evaluated for them. That is its own decision, tracked on metagraphed-infra#346.

## Template Used

- Backend/code change

author: rambaarde
body:
## Summary

Walked the whole flow as two people on two machines instead of reading it. Both defects land on **the teammate's first morning** — the one path that decides whether any of this works.

### The memory was created on the wrong branch

`git init` uses `init.defaultBranch`, which is still `master` unless someone changed it. So the memory was created on `master` and pushed to `master`, while GitHub and every other host point HEAD at `main`.

A teammate cloning got the remote's **empty `main`** and was told:

> `…` does not look like a varve memory (no _company.md)

Nothing in that message points at a branch. Now created on `main` via `symbolic-ref` — works on every git version and renames nothing on a repo with no commits.

### Empty was reported as malformed

A clone that succeeds and finds no `_company.md` is almost always a memory **nobody has pushed yet**. It now says so and names the fix, instead of sending a new teammate to inspect a repo that is simply empty.

## Test plan

- [x] `npm test` — **116 passing**, badge updated
- [x] **Full two-machine walkthrough**: owner `init` → `add` → commit → push; teammate clones only the code repo on a cold $HOME and `varve brief` fetches the memory and prints the briefing with nothing installed
- [x] Both failure paths checked by hand — unpushed remote, and a remote that does not exist
- [x] Regression tests: the memory is on `main`; an empty remote reports as unpushed
- [x] Re-verified `brief`, `notify` and the MCP server after touching `store.ts`

author: denisvmedia
body:
Refs #1206.

## Reproduced first, end to end, before a line changed

`go build -o <scratch>/bin/ptah-compat ./cmd/ptah-compat` on a clean tree, compared against `/Users/buster/Work/denis/ptah-atlas-conformance/bin/atlas` (self-reported `atlas community version v1.3.0`), invoked by absolute path. Every command was run unpiped into its own file with `$?` read on the next line, so no exit code belongs to a pipe stage. Fixtures were copied out of `internal/atlasmigrateimport/testdata/ce-sums/flyway/{no-separator,minor-version-ordering,leading-zero}` and `.../golang-migrate/basic`, each with the `atlas.sum` the community binary wrote, so both binaries read through the same integrity gate.

Every cell in the issue reproduces, value for value:

| cell | community v1.3.0 | ptah-compat, before |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `migrate apply` | exit 0, rows `1\|` `2\|ok` | exit 0, rows `4611686018427469511\|` `4611686018427510315\|ok` |
| `migrate set 1` | exit 0, `Current version is 1 (1 set)` | **exit 1**, `migration with version "1" not found`, no revision table |
| `migrate set 4611686018427469511` | **exit 1**, not found | **exit 0**, records it |
| `migrate set 1.5` | exit 0, `+ 1 (a)` `+ 1.5 (b)` | exit 1, `--version "1.5" is not a valid migration version: strconv.ParseInt` |
| `migrate set 01` | exit 0, row `01\|a` verbatim | exit 1, `migration with version "1" not found` |
| `migrate lint --latest 1` | `Analyzing changes from version 1 to 2` | `Analyzing changes from version 4611686018427469511 to 4611686018427510315` |
| `migrate status` | `Current Version: 2` | `Current Version: 4611686018427510315` |
| `migrate import` | `1.sql` `2_ok.sql` | `4611686018427469511.sql` `4611686018427510315_ok.sql` |
| control, golang-migrate `apply` and `set 1` | exit 0, `1\|init` | exit 0, `1\|init` — identical |

## What this changes

**`migrate set` on a converted Flyway directory takes the SOURCE version token.** The int64 ordering key `internal/atlasmigrateimport` projects that token onto stops being an accepted spelling.

The third row of the table above is why this is the part that had to move first. `migrate set 4611686018427469511` exited 0 here and exits 1 on the binary being mirrored — ptah-compat accepting what that binary refuses is the one direction the parity rule never allows, and it was the *only* spelling that worked. Nothing else in the measured set is in that direction.

Matching is measured, not inferred. The token is compared BYTE FOR BYTE, which the zero-padded fixture is what separates:

```
V01__a.sql, V2__b.sql        community v1.3.0
  migrate set 01   -> exit 0, "Current version is 01 (1 set)", row 01|a
  migrate set 1    -> exit 1, migration with version "1" not found
  migrate set 002  -> exit 1, migration with version "002" not found
  migrate set 2    -> exit 0, "Current version is 2 (2 set)", rows 01|a and 2|b
```

So `1` deliberately fails to reach `V01__a.sql`, and the index is a plain string key with nothing that normalizes.

The `Current version is ...` summary and the `+ N (desc)` lines render the same spelling, so on the fixtures above ptah-compat's stdout is now byte-identical to the community binary's.

The not-found message quotes the operand as typed. Measured: the community binary answers `migration with version "abc" not found` and `migration with version "0" not found` on a Flyway directory, where ptah answered `--version "abc" is not a valid migration version: strconv.ParseInt...` and `--version must be greater than zero` — diagnostics about int64 parsing on a directory that has no int64 versions.

**The #1100 refusal now prints a command that runs.** `foreignFlywaySetRoute` offered `migrate set <ordering key>` as the way forward. After this change that command is refused, so the refusal prints the token. The three tests that *execute* what the refusal prints, rather than only matching it, are what caught this — see the killed mutants below.

## Re-measured after the change

Same harness, same binaries, same fixtures. Every `migrate set` cell matches on exit code AND on stdout:

| operand | fixture | community | ptah-compat, after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `1` | V1.sql, V2__ok.sql | 0 | 0, stdout identical |
| `2` | V1.sql, V2__ok.sql | 0 | 0, stdout identical |
| `4611686018427469511` | V1.sql, V2__ok.sql | 1 | 1, stderr identical |
| `7` / `0` / `abc` | V1.sql, V2__ok.sql | 1 | 1, stderr identical |
| `1.5` | V1__a, V1.5__b, V2__c | 0 | 0, stdout identical |
| `15` | V1__a, V1.5__b, V2__c | 1 | 1, stderr identical |
| `01` | V01__a, V2__b | 0 | 0, stdout identical |
| `1` | V01__a, V2__b | 1 | 1, stderr identical |
| `2` | V01__a, V2__b | 0 | 0, stdout identical |
| **control** `1` | golang-migrate basic | 0 | 0, stdout identical, row `1\|init` |

The golang-migrate control is what separates "converted directories are addressed by token" (false) from "the Flyway projection is addressed by token" (true). It is pinned as `TestCompatMigrateSet_PlainPrefixLayoutsAreUnchanged` rather than only re-measured by hand. There is exactly one layout gate, inside `atlasmigrateimport.FlywayCoveredSourceVersions`, which reports nothing for the plain-numeric-prefix layouts.

One cell still diverges on message only, and it is untouched and pre-existing: `migrate set abc` on a **golang-migrate** directory. Both exit 1; the community binary says `migration with version "abc" not found` and ptah says `--version "abc" is not a valid migration version`. Fixing that means changing the native Atlas directory path too, which is not this issue.

## Mutation coverage

Each mutant was applied to the shipped source, the tests run, and the source restored. Nothing was staged while a mutant was in the tree.

1. **`resolve` never consulted** (`if tokens.translates()` → `if false`): 8 of the 10 rows of `TestCompatMigrateSet_ConvertedFlywayTakesTheSourceToken` FAIL, including `the_ordering_key_is_no_longer_an_accepted_spelling` and `dotted_token_is_addressable_at_all`.
2. **numeric normalization instead of a byte-exact match** (fall back to `ParseInt` on both sides of the lookup): exactly the two rows mutant 1 left alive FAIL — `a_zero-padded_token_is_not_reachable_by_its_numeric_value` and `a_plain_token_is_not_reachable_by_a_zero-padded_spelling`. The two mutants partition the table; neither rule is held by the other's rows.
3. **`render` never translates** (return `strconv.FormatInt` unconditionally): the four accepted rows FAIL on stdout, and so does `TestCompatMigrateSet_ConvertedDirWritesConvertedVersion`.
4. **the refusal prints the ordering key again** (`operand := strconv.FormatInt(head, 10)`): `ForeignFlywayRefusalPrintsWorkingRecovery`, `ForeignFlywaySetRouteOfferedWithPendingAboveTheHead` and `ForeignFlywayBaselineOverForeignHistory` FAIL — they run the printed command.

The test-style gate was also proved to be running rather than reporting: adding one `if` to a test body turns `scripts/check-test-style.sh` red with `new test conditional violations: cmd/atlas/migrate_set_flyway_version_test.go`, and removing it turns it green again.

## What this does NOT settle, and why it stops here

**The recorded `atlas_schema_revisions.version` column still holds the ordering key.** After `migrate set 1` the row is `4611686018427469511|`, where the community binary writes `1|`. `migrate apply`, `migrate lint`, `migrate status` and `migrate import` still print and write the key. Re-measured after this change, all of those are exactly as the issue describes them.

Recording the token means making migration identity in `migration/migrator` a string rather than an int64, and that package is public (`docs/public_api.md`). Concretely, the surface that would have to change:

- `Migration.Version int64`, `MigrationFile.Version int64`, `MigrationRevision.Version int64`, `MigrationStatus.CurrentVersion/TargetVersion/Versions`, `AtlasRevisionSetResult.CurrentVersion`, `AtlasRevisionChange.Version` — the identity type itself.
- `Migrator.SetAtlasRevision(ctx, int64)`

author: coenttb
body:
Wave 1 of the F16 port fleet (#404), class **C1b**, on the C0 contract (#429, `cd6b503c`).

**DO NOT MERGE.** The Python deletion is the second commit and is gated behind the `validate-base.yml` cutover PR per the coordinator's adjudication (comment 5214032437). The coordinator holds the gate.

## What lands

| rule | validator | retired script |
|---|---|---|
| `CI-010`, `CI-099` | `CI.Validation.CIMatrix` | `validate-ci-matrix.py` |
| `CI-021` | `CI.Validation.EmbeddedJob` | `validate-embedded-job.py` |
| `CI-102` | `CI.Validation.CompositeActionDescriptions` | `validate-composite-action-descriptions.py` |
| `CI-103` | `CI.Validation.EnvironmentContext` | `validate-env-context.py` |

Plus five sorted lines in `CI.Validation.Registry` and one test file. **No fixture is touched.**

Two of C1b's six listed members are not here. `CI-105` was already ported — C0 landed it as its proving member. `GH-REPO-063` is flagged unportable in this wave, with reasoning on #404 (comment 5214166355): it is not on the C0 contract and the manifest already records `migrate-to-base: no`, it has no fixture corpus so the unwaived comparison cannot be run, and half its predicate parses `validate-readme.py` with Python's `ast` — a file the port is deleting.

## The measured comparison

Retired script and Swift validator, run over **the full existing fixture corpus — all 304 scenario directories across all 68 rule corpora**, not only each rule's own. Both TSV streams filtered to the rule, sorted, byte-compared; exit codes compared under the normalised contract (0 = ran, 2 = could not run). **1,520 paired invocations.**

| rule | scenarios | findings | TSV | exit codes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `CI-010` | 304 | 113 | **byte-identical** | identical |
| `CI-099` | 304 | 2 | **byte-identical** | identical |
| `CI-102` | 304 | 2 | **byte-identical** | identical |
| `CI-103` | 304 | 3 | 2 of 3 byte-identical; 1 typed difference | identical |
| `CI-021` | 304 | 3 | **byte-identical** | identical |

Running each rule against every corpus rather than its own is what makes the `CI-010` row worth reading: 113 findings, because 20-odd unrelated corpora also carry a `swift-ci.yml`, and every one of them agrees.

### The one difference, typed

Scenario `gh-repo-074/fail/swift-unparseable-inline` holds a workflow with an unterminated flow sequence. Both implementations emit exactly one `CI-103` finding, against the same repository, under the same rule, citing the same file. Only the parser's own diagnostic text differs:

- retired: `` ci.yml: YAML parse failed: while parsing a flow sequence   in "<unicode string>", line 8, column 14: … ``
- ported: `` ci.yml: YAML parse failed: line 8: unsupported YAML construct — an unterminated flow sequence ``

This is not a predicate difference. It is PyYAML's exception string versus the C0 reader's refusal message, and C0 already settled the precedent — `Subject.workflows(citing:)` surfaces a refusal through `YAML.Error.message`. Reproducing PyYAML's wording would mean encoding a foreign parser's diagnostics as a contract. Recorded as a typed, explained difference per the methodology ruling.

## Design notes worth a reviewer's attention

**One validator for `CI-010` and `CI-099`.** Two readings of one file. The posture contrast is the substance: `linux-nightly` must be advisory because a nightly toolchain's instability is noise; `windows-release` must not be, because Windows is a target the ecosystem ships to and advisory-flipping it hides `#if os(Windows)` divergence. Reporting both under one identifier would let a Windows regression be triaged as toolchain noise.

**`CI-021` is narrower than `CI-105`, on purpose.** `CI-105` reads a quoted `"true"` as truthy; `CI-021` accepts only the boolean. They ask different questions — will Actions reject this shape, versus is the advisory posture actually declared. A string is not a declaration. The corpus's `embedded-coe-false` scenario is what holds the line, and there is a test for it.

**`CI-103` flags the `env` context and nothing else.** `inputs.*` and `vars.*` in `runs-on:`/`container:` are the recommended fix. A validator that flagged them would be flagging its own remedy.

**`CI-102` discovers actions locally.** It is the only member of this family that reads `.github/actions/` rather than `.github/workflows/`. Widening `Subject` for one consumer would put a shape in the shared contract nothing else asks for.

**`CI-010`'s messages keep their original quoting.** A finding message is a contract with whoever reads the check annotation; changing its punctuation mid-port would make a rewrite look like a behaviour change. The rendering is confined to one `fileprivate` extension at the bottom of that file, commented as what it is.

## Residues left deliberately

The four caller workflows still name the retired paths in `paths:` and `validator-script:`. Repointing that input is the **cutover PR's** decision — guessing at its shape would have to be undone. `validators-manifest.yaml` (5 entries) and `tests/scripts/run.sh` (4 cases) also still name them; `CI-MANIFEST-BINDING` check 2 is one-directional (every script on disk must be referenced, not every reference resolved), so the deletion does not make that gate fire. Those files belong to C5 and C0.

Posted by peer task `port-c1b`.

author: saurabhhhcodes
body:
## Description
This PR fixes real bugs found in the codebase:

- Replaced global `isNaN` with `Number.isNaN`: the global version coerces its argument, so `isNaN('1')` returns false while `Number.isNaN` is strict.
- Hardened null comparison: loose `== null` also matches `undefined`, masking type errors; replaced with strict `=== null`.
- Tightened `==` to `===`: loose equality performs type coercion, which can silently compare `0 == '0'` or `false == 0` as equal.
- Replaced global `isNaN` with `Number.isNaN`: the global version coerces its argument, so `isNaN('1')` returns false while `Number.isNaN` is strict.

- [x] Local manual testing

author: luther-rotmg
body:
## Summary

Bumps `ws` from `^8.16.0` (installed `8.19.0`) to `^8.21.2`, fixing two advisories:

- **[GHSA-58qx-3vcg-4xpx](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-58qx-3vcg-4xpx)** (HIGH — ws < 8.17.1) — **Uninitialized memory disclosure** via `cleanupBuffers`. A peer that sends a malformed frame can read up to ~65k bytes of adjacent Node heap memory back in the error response.
- **[GHSA-96hv-2xvq-fx4p](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-96hv-2xvq-fx4p)** (MODERATE — ws < 8.20.1) — **Memory-exhaustion DoS** via tiny fragmented frames + data chunks.

Both are patched in `ws >= 8.20.1`; this PR lands us at 8.21.2 (latest 8.x, no breaking changes vs 8.19.0).

## Blast radius

The realm-engine client's MITM proxy is the direct consumer of `ws`. The memory-disclosure CVE is the one that matters here — an unfriendly server could return heap bytes from the client's process on a malformed frame. Even if the RotMG production server is trusted, the "MITM proxy" position means the client accepts frames whose ultimate origin is variable (any upstream Deca puts behind their edge, plus any private/community server the user configures via server-switch or ip-connect).

## Surgical diff

Only `ws` changed in the lockfile — 105-package install tree is otherwise identical:

```diff
    "node_modules/ws": {
-     "version": "8.19.0",
+     "version": "8.21.2",
```

No consumer code required changes (the ws API surface within 8.x is stable — this is a patch-level bump within 8.x from the consumer's perspective).

## Follow-up PRs planned

`npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high` on this workspace still reports 4 more highs after this PR merges. Each is a bigger jump and gets its own PR with a compat review:

- `electron-updater ^6.3.9` → `^9.7.0` — **HIGH** [GHSA-p2f4-r6v6-j797](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p2f4-r6v6-j797) (`Authorization` header leaked on cross-origin redirect). Three majors — needs to check `AppUpdater` API changes and `electron-builder` compat.
- `sharp ^0.33.5` → `^0.35.0` — **HIGH** [GHSA-f88m-g3jw-g9cj](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f88m-g3jw-g9cj) (inherited libvips CVEs). Minor within 0.x — needs quick smoke test of the sprite pipeline.
- `fast-xml-parser ^4.3.0` → `^5.7.0` — **MODERATE** [GHSA-gh4j-gqv2-49f6](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gh4j-gqv2-49f6). MAJOR — output shape may differ.
- `js-yaml <=4.1.1` — transitive. Would come along with an `electron-builder` bump.

Once all four are in, PR #41 (CI locale-guard) becomes a natural home for an `npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high` job that keeps the tree clean.

author: whg517
body:
## What & why

#117 gave `page_text` and `page_snapshot` a `note` when a document draws its content into a
`<canvas>` — text tools return nothing there, and the note points at `page_screenshot`.

**Verified against the live site that motivated it. No note appeared at all.**

Notes are produced *per document*, but all three merges rebuild their result from scratch
and never copied `note` across:

```js
mergeSnapshot → { refCount, nodes, url, title }
mergeText     → { text, url, mode }
mergeLinks    → { links, count, url }
```

So the advisory survived only on single-frame pages. Two independent ways it was lost:

1. **Any sub-frame at all discarded the top frame's note**, since the merged object is built
   fresh — this is broader than canvas and affects every read op.
2. **`mergeText` appends a sub-frame's section only `if (t)`** — a frame whose text is empty
   is dropped entirely, taking its note with it. A canvas frame is exactly that: the canvas
   *is* the content, so `innerText` is empty.

Point 2 is the sharp one: **the note could only ever be lost in precisely the case it was
written for.**

### Isolation

Two fixtures differing only in framing, same 1460x2112 canvas:

| fixture | `page_text` result |
|---|---|
| canvas at top level | `keys: [mode, note, text, url]` — note present |
| canvas inside an iframe | `keys: [mode, text, url]` — **note gone** |

## The fix

`mergeNotes()` gathers the top frame's note and every sub-frame's, labels sub-frame ones
with their frame (knowing *which part* of the page is a canvas is most of the value), and
emits identical notes once. All three merges use it.

## Areas touched

- [x] Extension (background)
- [ ] Rust MCP server · Native host · Protocol · Permissions · Installer · Docs

## Tests

- [x] 7 new regression tests (119 total, was 112): a sub-frame note surviving an empty-text
  frame, the top note surviving the presence of sub-frames, dedup of identical notes, the
  field being omitted when there is nothing to say, and coverage for `mergeSnapshot` /
  `mergeLinks` which had the same hole
- [x] `make ci` green
- [x] **Verified in a real browser, twice**: the controlled fixture now returns
  `(frame f242) Part of this page is drawn into a <canvas> (1460x2112px)…`, and the original
  résumé page returns `(frame f233) … (1460x2184px) … use page_screenshot`. The résumé frame
  still contributes no text — the point is that its *note* now reaches the caller.

## Security-relevant?

- [x] Not security-relevant — advisory text propagation only.

## Housekeeping

- [x] CHANGELOG not touched — generated from commits since #119
- [x] ADR not needed

body:
# Pull Request

## Type of change

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] New feature
- [ ] Refactor / internal cleanup
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Other:

## Description of the changes

The Makefile's `-ldflags` injected `main.Version` / `main.Build` / `main.BuildDate`
/ `main.Branch` — none of which exist in `cmd/server` — so the linker silently
discarded all four and every `make build` reported the hardcoded fallback in
`pkg/version`. It now injects `pkg/version.Version/Commit/Date`, the same three
symbols GoReleaser sets, making that package the single version source across
build paths. Adds `internal/releasegate`, run by a tag-only `version-gate` CI
job and by `make version-check TAG=vX.Y.Z`, which refuses a release whose
`pkg/version` fallback doesn't match the tag being cut.

## Motivation for the changes

Partially addresses #97 (the "hardcoded `0-alpha.1`" defect; the install-path
footer and the `version` field on `GET /` are not in this PR).

Two build paths never receive GoReleaser's ldflags — `go install ...@vX.Y.Z` and
the docker image, which builds with no ldflags at all — so both report whatever
`Major`/`Minor`/`Patch` is compiled into `pkg/version/version.go`. That value had
drifted to `0-alpha.1` while the latest tag was `v0.1.0-alpha.3`. Fixing the
injection makes local builds honest; the gate stops the compiled fallback from
silently going stale again.

author: ziadzakaria76
body:
A value the parser could not have read correctly currently **removes the tender**, and says nothing about it.

## The problem

`_passes_value()` applies `MIN_VALUE_USD` to whatever came out of the parser. A number picked off the wrong fragment of a page — `"Published: 01 August 2026"` parsing to `1.0` — falls under the floor, and the tender leaves the report under **"below minimum value"**.

That is the same reason a genuine $50k tender gets. Nothing in the output separates *a scraper reading the wrong element* from *a market with no large tenders in it*. The pipeline shrinks and nothing fails.

Reproduced on `main` before changing anything:

| Record | Result on `main` |
|---|---|
| value parses to `1.0` | **dropped** as "below minimum value" |
| value parses to `9e12` | **kept**, reported at nine trillion dollars |
| genuine $50k tender | dropped (correct) |
| value not published | kept and flagged (correct) |

## The change

`_repair_implausible_value()` runs before any filter reads the value, and blanks anything outside `MIN_PLAUSIBLE_VALUE_USD..MAX_PLAUSIBLE_VALUE_USD`, attaching a flag saying the published value was not usable.

The tender then follows the unknown-value path that `KEEP_UNKNOWN_VALUE` already handles correctly, so it survives to be judged on everything else, and the parsing problem is visible in the report rather than only in the logs. The generic `"Value not published"` flag is suppressed in that case — the record already explains itself, and two flags saying overlapping things reads as noise.

This is the same idea `utils.dates` already applies to the other half of the record: `_plausible()` discards a date that parsed but cannot be true. Dates were covered; values were not.

## Scope

Deliberately narrow.

- Date plausibility is left alone — `PLAUSIBLE_YEARS` already handles it, and duplicating that here would be worse than leaving it.
- The business floor keeps working on its own terms: a real **$50k tender is still dropped**, and a **$900m programme is not called implausible**.
- A value exactly at the plausibility floor is treated as credible; it is the business floor that removes it, and keeping those two reasons distinct is the point of the change.

## Tests

Two added to the pipeline suite and registered in `TESTS`. **865 checks pass**, pyflakes clean.

While writing them I hit two things worth noting for anyone reading the diff: the tests initially did not run at all, because this suite uses an explicit `TESTS` registry rather than name-based discovery; and the first version failed because four records sharing the default title were fuzzy-deduplicated into one by `process()`, so the fixtures now carry distinct titles.

body:
## What this does

A sweep of every markdown file in the repository, then the consolidation asked for: one standing vision
document, an archive for the reading behind it, and a lean agent file.

**Nothing was completely stale.** The doc set is unusually well maintained — supersessions are recorded rather
than silently edited, and the cross-references are live. Exactly one file was dead by its own admission, and
the real staleness was at paragraph level.

## The one thing that was actually wrong

`docs/README.md` still asserted **"Mazing or preset path? — settled: no mazing, ever"** and described the
one-hex corridor as the playfield. [PR #71](https://github.com/ssalter21/tower-defense-game/pull/71) reversed
that the day before: the board is a maze again, at several elevation levels, with pathfinding owed to `sim/`.

That is the failure mode of keeping the same verdict in two files, so `docs/README.md` no longer carries
verdicts. It is an index now — what each document is *for*, and nothing a document could contradict.

## The layout

| | |
|---|---|
| `docs/vision.md` | The standing document. Destination, pillars, open questions, build order |
| `docs/decision-log.md` | **New.** Every reversal, with why. It grows; the vision should not |
| `docs/README.md` | An index. 22.8 KB → 8 KB, and no verdicts |
| `docs/archive/` | **New.** Parts I–V, each with a banner saying what survived it |
| `docs/research/` | Unchanged in scope; three notes gain a premise banner |
| `docs/adr/` | Untouched. It is the healthiest part of the set |

The reversal tables were 10% of the vision and growing weekly — two more landed on 6 August alone. §9 keeps the
Parts I–V table, because that is how you read `archive/` and it is stable; the self-revision tables moved out.

## The agent file

`CLAUDE.md` was 221 lines, of which **147 (66%) were a hot-reload timing measurement** — six tables of trial
data, loaded into every agent's context, that are a finding rather than an instruction.

- `AGENTS.md` — new, 76 lines: the four working agreements, the three practical Unity facts, and where things
  are written down. Rules only.
- `CLAUDE.md` — a pointer at it, so every tool reads the same file.
- `docs/research/unity-hot-reload-timing.md` — the measurement, with its tables intact.

12.7 KB of always-loaded context becomes 4.4 KB.

## Deleted

`tools/hotreload-probe/` — labelled throwaway in its own README, and the question it existed to answer
([#5](https://github.com/ssalter21/tower-defense-game/issues/5),
[#34](https://github.com/ssalter21/tower-defense-game/issues/34),
[#51](https://github.com/ssalter21/tower-defense-game/issues/51)) is answered. No solution file or project
referenced it.

## Also fixed while in there

- **Four stale anchors**, two of which predate this PR: `vision.md#one-purse` and
  `vision.md#4--the-balance-harness` both broke when those headings gained suffixes, and two notes pointed at
  `docs/README.md` sections that this PR removes.
- **The Sources list** in the vision had two `6`s and two `7`s.
- **An empty `### Research in flight` heading** — nothing is in flight, so it now says so.
- **The Rust-vs-C# open question** only lived in `docs/README.md`; it moves into the vision's §10 rather than
  disappearing with the section.
- **`docs/README.md` claimed the Element TD 2 tower-count correction was "not yet applied"** — it was applied
  by [#61](https://github.com/ssalter21/tower-defense-game/pull/61) on 3 August.

## Verification

- `dotnet build sim/sim.csproj` — clean.
- `dotnet test sim.tests` — **270 passed, 0 failed.**
- Every relative link in every tracked `.md` and `.html` resolved against the filesystem — **no broken links.**
- Every `#anchor` checked against its target file's headings — **no broken anchors** apart from the
  pre-existing `#s1`…`#s46` citation anchors, which are HTML `id` attributes rather than headings.

Docs-only: no `sim/`, `client/` or `tools/` behaviour changes, and the rebuilt plug-in binaries from the test
build were reverted rather than committed.

author: borovikvv
body:
## Что меняется

Из промпта исполнителя убрано требование создавать ветку `fix/issue-N`. Ветку заводит и публикует сам экшен, агенту переключаться запрещено явно.

## Зачем

Первый прогон на #204 отработал полностью: обе правки сделаны, `npm run lint`, `npx tsc -b`, `npm test` (979 тестов, 2 новых) и `npm run build` — зелёные. Но PR не появился.

Причина в логе:

```
Branch changed during chat: expected opencode/issue204-20260807075950, now on fix/issue-204
```

Экшен создаёт свою ветку и в конце сверяет, что агент на ней остался. Промпт велел перейти в другую — экшен увидел несоответствие и отказался публиковать. Работа уехала вместе с контейнером, в issue остался только текст описания.

## Что может сломаться

Имена веток станут вида `opencode/issue204-<timestamp>` вместо `fix/issue-204`. Соглашение из `CLAUDE.md` про `<тип>/issue-N` продолжает действовать для веток, которые заводим мы сами; у исполнителя формат диктует экшен, и спорить с ним дороже, чем принять.

## Проверка

Снять и заново повесить метку `ready-for-code` на #204: должны появиться ветка и PR, а в нём — `@claude review`.

author: avitsrimer
body:
## Summary

`bb pullrequest merge` now requires an interactive `y`/`N` confirmation
(`Merge pullrequest <id>? [y/N]`) with **no `--force`** of any kind — merging is
deliberately not automatable via `bb`.

- `common.ConfirmInteractive` (in `internal/common/confirm.go`) shares its prompt/read
  body with `Confirm` via a new unexported `promptYesNo` helper, but never reads a
  "force" flag, and treats an EOF with no input at all (e.g. `/dev/null` on stdin) as
  an error rather than `Confirm`'s silent decline.
- `mergeProcess` is gated on it after `WhatIfPayload`, before the async/sync split, so
  `--dry-run` behaves exactly as before.
- Declining prints `Merge canceled` (via `cmd.OutOrStdout()`) and exits `0`. A
  non-interactive or EOF stdin errors with `cannot confirm merge: ...: merging requires
  an interactive terminal`.
- README/CLAUDE.md/SKILL.md updated to document the stdin contract and steer an agent
  toward surfacing the ready-to-merge state and handing the actual merge off to a human
  instead of invoking the command itself.

## Breaking change

Any script or agent that piped stdin into, or ran under `/dev/null`/`nohup` with, `bb
pullrequest merge` now gets a non-zero exit instead of an unattended merge.

author: robertlemke
body:
Flow registers all classes found in the Tests/Functional directory of a package for object management when it runs in the Testing context. The tests of this package are plain PHPUnit tests which do not need Flow at all, but they were picked up nevertheless, and since version 2.4.0 they use PHP attributes provided by PHPUnit 10.

As a result, Flow applications which still use PHPUnit 9 could not boot in the Testing context anymore and failed with `Attribute class "PHPUnit\Framework\Attributes\Test" not found`. Note that Flow 9.1 itself still requires PHPUnit 9 for its own test infrastructure, so this affects current distributions.

The tests are integration tests - they require a running Redis server - and live in Tests/Integration now, where Flow does not look for classes.

author: kiki830621
body:
Refs #344

## Summary

[#317](https://github.com/PsychQuant/che-apple-mail-mcp/issues/317) removed a real injection by moving the mailbox filter from `LIKE` patterns over the **raw** URL to exact Swift comparisons over the **decoded** path. Two semantics changed with it, and nothing pinned either:

- **(A)** SQLite's `LIKE` is ASCII-case-insensitive by default. The replacement is exact, so `mailbox: "inbox"` stopped matching `INBOX` on all three fast paths — a name RFC 3501 §5.1 makes case-insensitive *by spec*, now returning a silent zero.
- **(C)** `MailboxURL.decode` percent-decodes the whole path at once, so a mailbox literally **named** `R&D/Sent` (raw `R%26D%2FSent`) is indistinguishable from the hierarchy `R&D` → `Sent`. `hasSuffix("/Sent")` pulled it into a `Sent` query — over-matching, the exact class #317 existed to kill, re-entering from the decode side.
- **(B)** The account filter's case-sensitive `url.contains` is the same regression's second door.

One rewrite, not three patches: components must exist before "the leaf" can be defined, and the case question cannot be *stated* until then.

## What changed

- **`MailboxURL.pathComponents`** splits the **encoded** path first and decodes each piece, so a `%2F` can never pose as a separator. `mailboxPath` is untouched — it is what `search_emails` reports and has 15 references across 6 files.
- **`mailboxPathMatches`** goes component-wise. Three of #317's four clauses turn out to be **one** predicate: *the query's components occur as a contiguous run inside the path's*. Full-path is the run spanning everything, leaf is the run at the end, descendant is a run that stops short. Strings needed four spellings only because they could not see where a component began.
- **Case policy** — `INBOX` folds (ASCII-only, not a Unicode fold); everything else exact; the hex account UUID folds.
- **Near-miss diagnostic** — an empty resolution with a case-only or whitespace-only candidate throws naming it instead of returning `[]`.

## The case policy diverges from what the issue proposed — on purpose

Blanket folding restores the old behavior bug-for-bug, but that behavior was accidentally lax, not correct: RFC 3501 makes only `INBOX` case-insensitive, other names are implementation-dependent and typically case-sensitive. On such a server `Work` and `work` are two mailboxes, and folding hands back the wrong one's mail.

The asymmetry decides it. **A miss is an empty result you go and investigate. A wrong hit is content you use.** So exactness wins — and what makes exactness affordable is the near-miss throw, which turns #317's own subject ("a zero you cannot trust") into a named answer without loosening what actually matches.

## Review-worthy judgment calls

**The surviving fourth clause is an accepted ambiguity.** Exact whole-path equality still runs against the lossy `mailboxPath`, so `R&D/Sent` resolves **both** the literally-named mailbox and the hierarchy. They are indistinguishable in the only representation the caller has, so picking one would be arbitrary; dropping the clause would make a slash-containing mailbox unreachable by any query.

**The near-miss is a closed enumeration** — ASCII letter case and outer whitespace, with no third class to be inferred by resemblance. A general similarity rule would decide on its own that `NoSuchBox` resembles something and turn a legitimately empty filter into an error. Implemented instead as *re-run the same matcher with a laxer component key*, so "near" cannot drift away from "matches".

**One file beyond the diagnosis's scope.** `Server.swift`'s `list_emails` catch would have swallowed the verdict and fallen through to AppleScript, leaving the diagnostic inert on one of three paths. That catch is for infrastructure failure; a near-miss is a semantic answer. It now rethrows that one case.

## Tests

**1135 total, 0 failures** (main baseline 1124 + 11 new). RED was verified against the unchanged matcher after the pure-addition API landed: **8 of 11 failed**, and the three that passed are the no-regression pins (`pathComponents`, exact-full-path round-trip, honest zero, descendant/leaf). All six `MailboxFilterTests` stay green — including `testLiteralUnderscore_doesNotWildcardMatch`, which pins #317's injection fix.

## Checklist
- [x] Diagnose
- [x] Implement (1 commit)
- [ ] Verify (run /idd-verify #344)
- [x] **Verify-gated**: post-verify PASS = ready to merge → after merge, run /idd-close to finalize this issue (manual gate + closing summary; no auto-close trailer)

Sister issue filed: #358 (`MailboxURL.mailboxName` carries the same `%2F` defect as dead code).

author: ashfulcra
body:
coord-opus-worker's P0. Reproduced, fixed, and regression-tested against a real shallow clone.

## The defect

`git cat-file -e` answers **"is this object HERE"**, not **"does this object EXIST"**. In a clone that legitimately does not hold all history those are different questions — and `review gc` treats a `False` as authoritative grounds to **retire a review**.

Reproduced against a real `--depth 1` clone, probing `af50075d` — the merged head of PR 546, unambiguously alive on `origin/main`:

```
$ git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository
true
$ git cat-file -e af50075d…^{commit}
fatal: Not a valid object name af50075d…          (rc 128)
```

The classifier maps `"not a valid object"` → `False`. So a **live head reads as affirmatively dead and gc destroys the review.** Same shape for a partial/promisor clone, where absence means "not fetched yet."

The existing docstring already said *"a broken repo must not retire a review"* — the intent was right. A shallow clone just isn't a *broken* repo; it's a healthy one that legitimately lacks objects, and nothing distinguished the two.

## The fix

The probe now establishes whether **this repository is capable of proving absence at all** — not shallow, no promisor remote, no partial-clone filter — and returns `None` when it is not.

Anything undeterminable counts as cannot-prove. This is the destructive path: an unnecessary `None` costs one more cycle with a review left open; a wrong `False` costs the review.

**Presence is unaffected.** A shallow clone still confirms the objects it holds, so gc keeps working on what it can actually see.

## Tests

Three, each against a **real depth-1 clone** rather than a mock:

1. absence reads **UNKNOWN** (the regression);
2. presence still reads **True** — the guard must not blind the probe;
3. a full clone still reads **False** — the over-correction guard, without which gc could never retire anything and the register rots, which is the problem gc exists to solve.

**Control:** the regression test fails against pre-fix `cli.py` and passes with it. Full `coord-engine` run: 25 failures, identical to baseline (pre-existing environment leakage).

## Note on blast radius

Worth stating plainly: cloud and CI harnesses commonly clone shallow. This is not a hypothetical configuration — it is the default in several places gc could plausibly run.

author: cevheri
body:
Closes #288. Closes #279.

Three deferred items, triaged by what each one costs a reader rather than by how much work it is. **No behaviour changes** — a deprecation tag, a backlog entry and a module header.

The context: these three are not scheduled while the product's attention is elsewhere. Leaving them open unanswered for months is its own cost, but so is closing a defect that still bites. So they are not treated the same way.

## #288 — the flag now says it does nothing

`WorkspaceFeatures.inlineEditing` is declared in a published interface, a host can set it, and nothing reads it: `StudioWorkspace` hard-codes `editingEnabled={false}` at both grid call sites, and the embedded query adapter's `executeQuery` takes no execution options, so it could not carry the `skipSafety` flag the standalone inline-edit path relies on (#269) even if a caller reached it.

The issue offered two resolutions — remove the field, or implement it. Both are wrong right now: removing it stops every host that sets it from compiling, and implementing it waits on #279. So this takes the option the issue was actually asking for. Its own words are that "a declared capability that is neither implemented nor rejected is the state to avoid" — this **rejects** it, explicitly, where a host reads the contract.

Verified in the built package rather than assumed: the tag lands on the field in `dist/workspace.d.ts`, so a host's editor strikes it through and says why.

## #279 — moved to `docs/BACKLOG.md` and closed

Deferred work, not a defect. #269 already made the software honest about it: the `supportsInlineRowEdit` capability hides the control wherever the shared `UPDATE <table> SET <col> = <val> WHERE <pk> = <val>` shape does not fit, so nothing is broken and no user is misled — the feature is simply absent on ClickHouse, Druid, MongoDB, Redis, Couchbase and the embedded engine.

The backlog entry keeps everything the issue knew: the per-provider forms (ClickHouse's `ALTER TABLE … UPDATE`, MongoDB's document path, append-only engines keeping the capability false), the provider-triad obligation, and the two constraints inherited from #269 — one request per edited row, and primary-key detection that should come from the schema rather than from column names. It also records that whether row editing should be universal at all is a product decision.

That is a **demotion**, the reverse of the file's documented promote-to-an-issue rule, so the rule now states both directions and where the line falls:

> An issue that is understood, breaks nothing today and is not scheduled belongs here rather than in a tracker where it only ages […] A defect a user can hit stays an issue — closing one of those hides a limitation instead of deferring it.

## #284 — stays open, and the generator now states its gap

Not closed, and not backlogged. The schema-diff generator can emit migration SQL that is unrunnable outside PostgreSQL — a `BEGIN;`/`COMMIT;` wrapper that MSSQL cannot parse and Oracle reads as a PL/SQL block, `ADD COLUMN`/`DROP COLUMN` in one shape for eleven type ids, and `DROP INDEX IF EXISTS` fallbacks Oracle rejects. A user meets that as broken SQL, so it keeps its issue; closing it would hide a limitation rather than defer it.

What it lacked was any statement of the gap where a developer meets it. `generateMigrationSQL(diff, dialect)` takes a dialect whether or not the path in question uses one, so the partial coverage is invisible from a call site. The module header now names the one path that is dialect-aware (the modified-column path, #269) and the four that are not.

The issue itself is getting a `help wanted` label and a comment recording that it is unscheduled, well specified, and that the emitted forms want checking against a live MSSQL and Oracle before they are settled — the way #264 and #265 were.

## Verification

`bun run format` · `bun run lint` (0 errors; no warning touches either changed source file) · `bun run typecheck` · `bun run knip` · `bun run test` (exit 0) · `bun run build` · `bun run build:lib` + `bun run attw` · `bun run coverage:check` → **29254/29254 lines (100.00%)**.

No tests were added: nothing executable changed. The one claim worth checking mechanically — that the deprecation reaches consumers — was checked against the built `dist/workspace.d.ts`.

author: zackees
body:
Closes #2316.

## Problem

`describe_root_ownership_conflict` (`crates/soldr-daemon/src/daemon/lifecycle/mod.rs`) has three arms. The orphan-with-missing-image arm `(alive, image_exists) = (true, false)` is actionable — it names the PID and says *"terminate PID {pid} to recover."* But the arm that fires when the **recorded owner is dead yet acquisition still failed** — i.e. a *different*, unrecorded process holds the filesystem lock — dead-ended:

```
soldr root ownership is busy: … (recorded PID N is not alive; the lock is held by an unrecorded process)
```

No culprit, no remediation, no next step. In the field this is the common orphan shape (a backgrounded build whose parent shell exited, or a version rotation that left an older `soldr-daemon` holding the OS lock while the PID file names a since-dead process). Every compile then silently degrades to direct rustc, and the only recovery is to discover and kill the orphan by hand.

## Fix

Make the `(false, _)` arm actionable, mirroring the `(true, false)` arm the codebase already ships:
- name the culprit **class** — an orphaned `soldr-daemon` that outlived the PID file;
- explain why soldr can't name the exact holder here, and why `soldr daemon stop` can't reach it (it probes the pipe, not the lock — soldr#1987);
- hand over the platform-specific command to list and terminate the orphan(s): `Get-Process soldr-daemon | Stop-Process -Force` (Windows) / `pkill -f soldr-daemon` (unix), noting daemons are respawned on demand so it's safe.

The function stays **pure** (no process enumeration / no side effects), so its three existing unit tests keep calling it directly; enumeration would have made it impure and CI-flaky, and the core complaint was the missing *remediation*, which this delivers.

## Test

New `a_dead_recorded_owner_points_at_the_orphan_remediation` (uses the `i32::MAX as u32` dead-PID idiom already established in these lifecycle tests) asserts the message now carries `soldr#2316`, names the orphan class, and contains a platform-appropriate kill command. Full module: `soldr cargo test -p soldr-daemon --lib events::` → 18 passed.

Companion: #2317 (the daemon-unavailable marker that replays this arm's text as `prior_failure`).

author: typeless
body:
putup declines to generate a dependency scan for commands it cannot reproduce — correctly — and says nothing. This makes it say something.

**Refs #352. It does not close it**: this change makes the problem visible; the matcher fix is tracked there.

## What is silent today

`matches_gcc_compile` takes the compiler from the command's first word (or the second, behind a recognized wrapper). A compile that is not there is not recognized, so no scan node exists, so the rule's headers are never recorded — and nothing reports it:

```
: foo.c |> echo building %f && gcc -c %f -o %o |> %B.o
```

Build succeeds. Edit `foo.h`. `Nothing to do (up to date)` — the object is stale.

**That refusal is deliberate and should stay.** It was introduced by `dbdbffdbf` to fix a `build-gcc-bsp` CI failure, and it is pinned by three test sections. The reason is real: a scan node runs from the Tupfile's directory with the prefix stripped (`src/exec/scheduler.cpp` sets the job cwd from `SourceDir`), so a `cd /build && gcc -c …` scan would resolve `-I` paths and sources somewhere the compile never was. putup cannot reproduce arbitrary shell state and should not pretend to.

The defect is not the refusal. It is the silence.

## What this adds

A rule whose declared outputs include an object file, that no scanner matches and that carries no depfile flag, is now reported:

```
$ putup parse
binutils/Tupfile:0: warning: no dependency scan for '../build-gcc/binutils/bfd-archive.o':
  putup recognizes no compile it can reproduce in this command, so any header this rule reads
  goes unrecorded. Harmless if it preprocesses none — an assembler, a copy, a partial link.

$ putup -n
[build-gcc] 5 rules produce an object file with no dependency scan; run 'putup parse' for the list.
```

Per-rule findings live in `parse`; the build gets one summary line. A warning firing on every build trains people to scroll past warnings.

The predicate calls the production generator (`match_and_generate`) rather than re-deriving the match — a second call site of one implementation, not a second implementation. The first version keyed on scan nodes present in the graph and flagged **every** compile under `parse`, because `parse` never installs the scanner registry; that RED is why the check now asks the registry directly instead of reading the graph.

## Why the diagnostic ships before the matcher fix

Widening the matcher means deciding which command prefixes are harmless — a list, which is a convention that must track the shell forever. A convention with a silent failure mode is the thing this codebase keeps removing. Underneath a diagnostic it stops being silent: a harmless spelling not yet on the list degrades from *silent under-scan* to *reported under-scan*. The convention no longer fails quietly; it lags, and the diagnostic measures the lag.

So the diagnostic is the precondition for the allowlist being acceptable at all, which is why it lands first and separately.

## The population, declared rather than pending

Five rules, all `examples/bsp/binutils/Tupfile` for-loop batch compiles. Each now carries a comment saying why it has no scan and pointing at #358, so the list the summary advertises explains itself.

Precision worth stating: those rules compile 103 objects, but **CI builds them from scratch every run and therefore never observes the staleness**. The harm lands on incremental local builds of the BSP. "103 objects unscanned in CI" is true and reads as a CI correctness hole; it is not one.

A per-rule opt-out is **not** in this change. Every spelling is new Tupfile syntax — tup's per-rule attribute slot is the caret block, which putup deliberately rejects (#217) — so it is a design-gate question, filed as **#358** with four priced candidates. CI runs neither `parse` nor any assertion on the summary line, so shipping without it costs one line on a local BSP build.

## What it deliberately does not cover

Named here and in the spec prose rather than implied:

- **Compile-and-link rules with no `-c`** (six `HOSTCC` rules in the gmp example) produce executables, not objects, so the output-shaped trigger does not fire. A second silent class.
- **A depfile flag anywhere in the command text** suppresses the finding, even when it belongs to another invocation — `echo -MD && gcc -c %f` is silent where `echo building && gcc -c %f` is reported. Filed as **#357**; the honest predicate needs invocation splitting.
- The mid-command source fold (**#356**) and flag-folding staleness (**#355**) are separate, and `REQ-SCAN-FLAG-SOURCE` records that folding **as it is**, not as it should be.

## Parity residual, declared

The check passes `command`, `node_id` and `working_dir`; `outputs` and `inputs` stay empty — `outputs` because the graph exposes no `PathId` accessor (adding one is a graph API change that does not belong in a diagnostic PR), `inputs` because the graph's resolved paths are not the rule-value inputs production passes, and a wrong-shaped field is worse than an empty one. No scanner reads either field today (grep: zero hits on both). A scanner that starts consulting them will diverge from this check; the note now on `CommandInfo` itself is where that divergence would be authored.

## Spec

New `dep-scan` area, `putup-only` throughout (tup does no scanning, so no reference exists):

- **`REQ-SCAN-UNREPRODUCIBLE-PREFIX`** — the sentence whose absence let #352 be filed against a deliberate decision. `dbdbffdbf`'s reasoning stops being folklore in a test name.
- **`REQ-SCAN-FLAG-SOURCE`** — current behaviour, including that source words fold from every invocation *whether or not it runs a compiler* (`gcc -c a.c -o a.o && rm junk.c` emits `gcc -M a.c junk.c`).
- **`REQ-SCAN-REPORT-UNSCANNED`** — this change's own behaviour.

Two requirements were caught **false** while drafting and corrected before landing: the first claimed no scan when *any* word precedes the compiler (falsified by `ccache gcc -c`, which is scanned via the wrapper bump), and the second claimed folding from compiler invocations only. Both now say what the code does.

`REQ-SCAN-RECOGNIZE` is deliberately **held** — as drafted it is false today and would overclaim even after the matcher fix. It lands with that change, worded to its actual contract.

## Verification

RED then green for the diagnostic's three branches (reported / not reported / suppressed by own depfile), plus an assertion that **runs the command the summary advertises** and requires it to succeed — added after review caught the summary pointing at `putup parse --check`, a spelling putup rejects.

`make test` 780 cases (main: 779), `format`, `tidy`, `iwyu`, `spec-check` (5 areas, 87 requirements), `bootstrap-scripts` no drift.

## Note on the metrics comment

`Hash computations 0 (-100.0%)` is **not** this change, and the merge was held until that was measured rather than assumed.

That counter is the number of recorded files whose mtime lands within the one-second racy-clean window before the index was saved (`src/cli/cmd_build.cpp:283-285`, `:371-381`) — a property of the *preceding build's* wall-clock timing, not of the dry run. Measured four ways: a binary built from `main@6b3c4a93e`, with none of this PR's code present, produces `Hash computations: 0` on the same corpus; and both binaries produce byte-identical counters against an identical index, including on a corpus where the counter is non-zero and could have differed.

The deterministic parts of the report are unchanged: **Commands 3545, Stat calls 5884, Graph edges 381415, Implicit deps 344126, Files in index 6102.**

The metrics note's claim that a change in `hash_computations` is "a real behavior change, not noise" is itself wrong, and is filed as #361.

## Performance: what it costs, and what was rejected

CI's cachegrind instruction counts are deterministic — three prior PRs sat at byte-identical 1529 M / 2370 M. The first version of this change measured **parse +25.0%, dry-run +13.8%**, and the merg

author: 0kaba0
body:
First of the four in #1117. Closes the duplicate half of #1114 and makes the negative half structural rather than conventional.

## Collapsed at parse, and at write

Parse is the important one: it holds for files written by any past version, by hand, or by a tool we do not own. Write is there so a caller that assembled duplicates in memory cannot leave a file that reads back differently from what it believed it wrote.

## One decision I made and want reviewed: last wins, not union

A line is a statement about an identifier, and the later statement is the current one — the same thing a write means. Union is exactly the behaviour that made reduction impossible (`lrskxa` then `lr` resolving to `lrskxa`), so collapsing by union would have fixed the accumulation and left the defect. It also errs towards fewer rights where a file is ambiguous, which is the direction to err in.

The visible consequence is that this alone repairs the reduction case for files already on disk:

```
user=u2 lrskxa
user=u2 lr          -> effective "lr", and the file is rewritten as one line
```

So the CLI fix in #1114 stops being what stands between an operator and a working `acl set`. It is still worth doing for the reason you gave — the client should not own a canonical form the server defines — but it is no longer load-bearing.

## The negative half, structurally

At most one entry per identifier *per sign* means an identifier's negative mask is decided by one entry rather than by how many lines mention it. The test asserts the property rather than an example: the same ACL with the positive and negative lines in either order resolves the same.

Two lines of the *same* sign are order-dependent on purpose now — that is what last-wins means — and the test says so, so the next reader does not read the first property as contradicted.

## Not in this PR

Global precedence and the owner short-circuit, in that order, per your correction — the first because it is the one that errs towards granting. Neither is touched here.

Mutation-checked: collapse removed at parse fails with `entries = 2, want 1: "user=u2 lr\nuser=u2 sk\n"`.

author: krutagyakaneria
body:
## Summary

This PR makes order creation transactional, crash-safe, and durably idempotent.

Previously, order creation relied on Redis-based request idempotency while the order, initial timeline, and load offer could be created through separate database operations. This created failure windows where a process crash, Redis lock expiration, or request retry could result in partial domain state or duplicate orders.

This change moves correctness to the database layer by combining transactional order creation with durable idempotency while retaining Redis as an optimization where appropriate.

## Problem

The previous order creation flow could behave like:

```text
Request
   ↓
Redis Idempotency Lock
   ↓
Create Order
   ↓
Create Timeline
   ↓
Create Load Offer
   ↓
Store Result in Redis
```

Several failure windows existed.

For example:

```text
Order creation succeeds
        ↓
Timeline succeeds
        ↓
Load offer succeeds
        ↓
Database state committed
        ↓
Application crashes
        ↓
Redis result was never stored
        ↓
Client retries
        ↓
Duplicate order may be created
```

Compensating deletes could handle some caught exceptions but could not provide transaction guarantees when the application terminated unexpectedly.

## What Changed

### Transactional Order Creation

- Consolidated required order creation writes into a PostgreSQL transaction.
- Ensured the order, initial timeline, and initial load offer are committed as one logical operation.
- Prevented partial order state from surviving failed transactions.
- Preserved existing display-ID generation and collision handling.

### Durable Idempotency

- Introduced durable idempotency state for order creation.
- Associated idempotency records with the resulting domain operation.
- Added request fingerprint validation.
- Added completed-response/resource replay.
- Prevented the same idempotency key from representing different requests.

### Concurrent Request Protection

- Added database-level protection for simultaneous requests using the same idempotency key.
- Ensured exactly one order creation operation can win.
- Prevented Redis lock expiration from allowing duplicate order creation.

### Crash Recovery

- Made successful order creation discoverable after application/process failure.
- A retry after a successful database commit returns the existing operation rather than creating another order.
- Removed Redis availability from the core correctness guarantee.

### Redis Integration

- Retained Redis where useful for fast request coordination and caching.
- PostgreSQL durable state now acts as the authoritative idempotency boundary.
- Redis cache loss or lock expiration no longer permits duplicate domain creation.

### Data Integrity

- Replaced compensating deletion as the primary database atomicity mechanism.
- Ensured required order-related records remain transactionally consistent.
- Preserved existing order API behavior and authentication boundaries.

## New Creation Flow

```text
Create Order Request
        ↓
Idempotency Key + Fingerprint
        ↓
Durable DB Arbitration
        ↓
PostgreSQL Transaction
   ┌────┼───────────────┐
   │    │               │
 Order Timeline     Load Offer
   │    │               │
   └────┴───────┬───────┘
                ↓
      Idempotency Completed
                ↓
              COMMIT
                ↓
         Return Created Order
```

## Crash Recovery

```text
Database transaction commits
        ↓
Application crashes before response
        ↓
Client retries same key
        ↓
Durable idempotency record found
        ↓
Original operation/result returned
        ↓
No duplicate order
```

## Reliability Improvements

After this change:

- Order creation is atomic.
- Partial order/timeline/load-offer state cannot survive a failed transaction.
- Concurrent duplicate requests create exactly one order.
- Process crashes after commit do not cause duplicate orders.
- Redis lock expiration does not compromise correctness.
- Redis cache loss does not compromise correctness.
- Completed operations can be safely replayed.
- Idempotency keys cannot silently be reused with different payloads.
- Idempotency remains isolated between users.

## Testing

Added/updated coverage for:

- [x] Normal transactional order creation
- [x] Timeline creation failure and rollback
- [x] Load-offer creation failure and rollback
- [x] Sequential duplicate requests
- [x] Concurrent duplicate requests
- [x] Same key with different payload
- [x] Crash-after-commit recovery
- [x] Missing Redis state
- [x] Redis lock expiration
- [x] User-scoped idempotency
- [x] Display-ID collision handling
- [x] Database transaction rollback

## Type of Change

- [x] Distributed Systems / Reliability
- [x] Data Integrity
- [x] Transaction Safety
- [x] Idempotency Improvement
- [x] Backend Architecture
- [ ] Breaking Change

## Breaking Changes

None expected.

The existing order creation API remains compatible while gaining stronger transactional, concurrency, and retry guarantees.

## Related Issue

Closes #7493

##GSSoC
#ECSoC26

This PR is submitted as part of GirlScript Summer of Code (GSSoC) 2026.



## Impact

This PR closes critical failure windows between order creation, related database writes, and idempotency persistence.

Order creation now remains consistent across concurrent requests, Redis failures, request retries, process crashes, and partial database failures without producing duplicate orders or incomplete domain state.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **New Features**
  - Added reliable order creation retries using idempotency keys, preventing duplicate orders and replaying completed responses.
  - Added customer order history, active orders, details, timelines, bids, ratings, and marketplace load-offer retrieval.
  - Added delivery geofence confirmation and OTP confirmation support.
  - Added en-route offer ranking and improved load-offer caching.

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Improved order and payment operation reliability during temporary locking-service outages.
  - Strengthened validation, access checks, rate limits, and duplicate-request handling.
  - Improved cancellation behavior for orders at the drop-off stage.

author: morluto
body:
Follow-up to #600 (merged). PR #600 was squash-merged while the three open review threads below were still being addressed. This PR lands those fixes against `main` and resolves the threads.

## Fixes

**1. Decouple evidence, scope, and assurance diagnostics (`verifier.py`)**

When an otherwise correct submission had one schema-level envelope error (e.g. a wrong `scope`), `load_submission` returned `None`, so the `isinstance(s, dict)` guards marked independently valid `evidence`, `scope`, and `assurance` diagnostics as failed. Evidence, scope, and assurance are now derived from the bounded raw submission object (`raw`), while the strict contract (`c`) remains the aggregate protocol gate. A single envelope error no longer erases an independently valid dimension.

**2. Validate embedding values before set operations (`verifier.py`)**

When the bounded raw result contained an unhashable `local_to_original` mapping entry (e.g. a nested list), `set(mapping)` raised `TypeError` before `mathematics()` could return `False`. Because the raw diagnostic path invokes `mathematics` without schema filtering, the top-level exception handler then reported every dimension as zero — including a valid input binding — and reported `false_certification` as false even when the submission claimed `VERIFIED`. Each mapping element is now validated to be an exact `int` in `[0, 9)` before the `set()` construction, so an unhashable entry returns a clean mathematical failure (`mathematics: 0.0`) rather than crashing the verifier.

**3. Parse uncapped evidence without loading it all into memory (`verifier_support.py`)**

With `max_bytes=None`, `read_evidence_json()` resolved the artifact and then used `target.read_text()`, allocating the entire file before `json.loads` could reject it. A digest-correct answer JSON padded to more than the verifier's memory limit but less than the task's storage limit could OOM-kill the container before the `MemoryError` handler emitted `reward.json`, leaving schema-equivalent valid evidence without a deterministic result. `read_evidence_json` now streams the file through a bounded incremental reader (`_BoundedTextReader`) with a memory-safety ceiling (`MAX_EVIDENCE_JSON_BYTES = 64 MB`) that is far above any legitimate fixed-shape answer but well below the OOM threshold, parsing fixed-shape JSON with bounded memory rather than restoring an arbitrary evidence-size rejection.

## Verification

- `verifier.py` and `verifier_support.py` pass `ast.parse` syntax validation.
- All 4 existing validation tests pass (`test_reconstruction_deck_certificate.py`).
- New scenarios verified via the validation child runner:
  - **Fix 1**: a submission with a wrong `scope` now reports `evidence: 1.0`, `assurance: 1.0`, `scope: 0.0`, `mathematics: 1.0`, `aggregate_reward: 0.0` (previously `evidence/scope/assurance` all `0.0`).
  - **Fix 2**: a submission with an unhashable mapping entry now reports `mathematics: 0.0` with no verifier error (previously crashed with `TypeError` zeroing every dimension).
  - **Fix 3**: legitimate small evidence parses via the streamed reader; oversized digest-correct evidence is rejected with `None` rather than loading the whole file.

Dockerfile `jacobian.checksum` label refreshed to the new `verifier.py` sha256 (`b645d515…`).

author: takarevert
body:
## Summary

Adds the onboarding entrypoint repo: a root `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` manifest that routes an AI assistant between static content and live pointers, plus authored content for all five sections (Getting Started, Org & Teams, Business & Strategy, Architecture, Projects). Anyone building the product can now clone this repo and get answers about the product, org, architecture, business model, and strategy primarily by asking an AI assistant — nothing like this existed before.

## Key decisions

- Hybrid static/pointer split: slow-changing content (org structure, strategy) is authored here directly; fast-changing content (architecture, current projects, most business/strategy detail) stays a live pointer into its real source (4 GitHub repos, `revert-knowledge-base`, Linear) rather than a copy that goes stale.
- `revert-knowledge-base` — the company's existing internal knowledge base — is scoped via `git sparse-checkout`, not a full clone: only 5 specific paths are ever fetched, and its fundraising/sales/regulation/meeting-archive folders are permanently excluded, even from instructions that arrive inside fetched content itself.
- The 4 architecture repos get a secrets-screening instruction instead of path-scoping, since the assistant needs broad read access across them for architecture questions.
- WebFetch is explicitly not treated as a working fallback for these private repos without separate authentication — an unreachable primary mechanism reports as unreachable rather than silently trying an unauthenticated fetch.
- Org & Teams' per-repo ownership is inferred from commit history only (no CODEOWNERS/HR system existed to consult) and is labeled unconfirmed in the file itself, rather than presented as fact.

Session-settled decisions carried from planning: hybrid static/pointer split, full v1 scope, PR-driven maintenance, and `revert-knowledge-base` as a live-pointer source with sensitive folders excluded (user-directed); repo assumed private/internal (user-approved).

## Testing

No application test suite exists for this docs/manifest repo. The plan's Verification Contract (14 acceptance examples) plus a 5-reviewer `ce-code-review` pass stand in for it. Rather than reviewing the sparse-checkout mechanism on paper only, I ran the actual command sequence against the real `revert-knowledge-base` remote — twice, before and after a code-review fix — and confirmed the excluded folders never materialize and `GOLDEN_SOURCE_RULES.md` is readable without widening scope. Review caught, and I fixed, a real bug this way too: the original instructions omitted the `git checkout` step needed after a `--no-checkout` clone, which left the working tree empty (verified by actually hitting the bug, then the fix).

**Known residuals** (not blocking, tracked for follow-up):
- GitHub-unreachable and partial-access behavior (the plan's AE5/AE6) weren't exercised live this session.
- No acceptance example yet exercises the new fallback-on-tool-failure instruction.
- Content `owner` frontmatter fields are placeholder `TBD` pending a human assignment.
- Linear-sourced Projects content and registering this assistant as a 4th `revert-knowledge-base` consumer both remain deferred to a future working session, by design.

## New concepts

### Sparse-checkout as an access boundary, not just a performance tool

`git sparse-checkout` is usually reached for to keep large monorepo clones fast. Here it's the actual security mechanism: `AGENTS.md` tells the assistant to clone `revert-knowledge-base` with `--filter=blob:none --no-checkout`, then `sparse-checkout set --no-cone` naming only 5 permitted paths, then `git checkout` — so the 4 sensitive folders (fundraising, sales, regulation, meeting archives) are never materialized on disk at all, rather than being fetched and then hidden by an instruction not to look.

This is meaningfully stronger than an instruction-only exclusion, but it has a real limit worth knowing: sparse-checkout scopes the *working tree*, not git's object database — a command that directly names an excluded path (`git show <ref>:<path>`) can still retrieve it. That's why the assistant-behavior rule (never fetch or surface those paths, regardless of mechanism) still does the actual work; sparse-checkout narrows the blast radius of an assistant that follows the manifest correctly, it doesn't replace the behavioral rule.

Use this pattern when an AI assistant needs broad read access to a source that contains a few genuinely sensitive subtrees you can enumerate up front. Don't reach for it when sensitive content is scattered unpredictably through the tree — screening/redaction is the better fit there (see the 4 architecture repos' secrets-screening instruction in the same file for that alternative).

## Post-Deploy Monitoring & Validation

No runtime/production system is affected — this is a static content repo with no deploy step. Validation signal: early readers report the assistant answering correctly from Getting Started/Org & Teams/Architecture/Business & Strategy, without surfacing excluded `revert-knowledge-base` content. Failure signal: the assistant reports it can't reach `revert-knowledge-base` at all (a sparse-checkout regression), or — treat as urgent — a reader reports seeing fundraising/sales/regulation content surfaced. Rollback is a plain revert of the merge commit. Owner: whoever merges this PR; validation window: the first couple of weeks of real onboarding usage.

author: lucadeleo
body:
Closes #33.

`cat` stays the terse prose view; `structure` is the editing model — the raw `documents.get` response, so an agent can inspect a document and derive safe native mutation ranges without parsing Markdown. This is the foundation the issue author builds #34 (guarded batch), #37 (table edits), and #38 (native elements) on top of.

```bash
gdoc structure DOC                          # whole doc, compact JSON
gdoc structure DOC --verbose                # indented
gdoc structure DOC --tab Notes              # one tab's raw subtree + documentId/revisionId
gdoc structure DOC --fields 'revisionId,tabs(tabProperties)'
gdoc structure DOC --suggestions-view-mode preview_suggestions_accepted
```

## Acceptance criteria from the issue

- **Safe native mutation ranges**: the output is the unmodified API response — UTF-16 `startIndex`/`endIndex`, paragraph roles/styles, list state, tables and cell geometry, inline objects, named ranges, headers/footers, segment IDs all preserved. The command description and README call out the two index traps (UTF-16 code units, not Python offsets; a smart chip is one code unit).
- **Tab/segment identity retained**: tab content is always requested (`includeTabsContent=True`); `--tab TITLE|ID` returns that tab's raw subtree (tabProperties + documentTab + childTabs) alongside `documentId`/`revisionId` so ranges stay attributable. Resolution matches `resolve_tab` semantics (case-insensitive title first, then ID) via a new `resolve_raw_tab` helper that searches the whole child-tab tree.
- **Narrowing for large docs**: `--tab` and/or `--fields` (mask passed verbatim; help notes Google rejects masks that recursively expand `childTabs` — our #14).
- **Suggestions mode is explicit**: `--suggestions-view-mode` accepts the four enum values; since the mode changes content *and* indexes, the mode used is echoed in the output (the API echoes it natively; if a fields mask strips it, an explicitly requested mode is re-added).
- **Read-only + state flow**: runs pre-flight, rejects spreadsheets (exit 3), and counts as a full read for the awareness baseline (`last_read_version`), same as `cat`.

Output is always JSON: compact by default (token economy), `--verbose` indents, `--json` wraps in the standard `ok` envelope.

## Verification

- 18 new tests (1255 total on this branch, all passing); ruff clean on touched code.
- Live smoke test: full dump (documentId/revisionId/tabs present), `--tab "Tab 1"` narrowed subtree with correct `startIndex`, `--fields 'revisionId,title'` verbatim mask worked with tab content requested, `--suggestions-view-mode preview_without_suggestions` echoed. Scratch doc deleted.

Note: independent branch off main; version 0.17.0 (0.15.0 = PR #41, 0.16.0 = PR #42). Merging in order; the later ones get a trivial CHANGELOG/version rebase at merge time.
